newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Canada says most nations want troops in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Canada says most nations want troops in Zaire.

text.p: Canada said on Wednesday most nations involved in the humanitarian crisis in eastern Zaire believed a military force was still needed to deliver aid to Rwandan refugees.
But Ottawa's Deputy Foreign Minister Gordon Smith said military planners needed to develop a range of options -- including not sending ground troops at all.
Smith spoke at a news conference after a series of meetings at the United Nations, one of which involved representatives from 60 countries, including states who volunteered troops.
"Virtually all countries, including Zaire ... believe that a military force is still required," he said.

"The conclusions of the meetings today are that the military planners need to develop options," he said. "The options of course include a zero option -- that there is no need for a military force to provide security to humanitarian relief organizations."

The options, he said, ranged from convoys and air support that might not require ground troops to a scaled-down version of the original intervention plan that a week ago envisaged at least 10,000 soldiers in the region.

In Ottawa, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said that the need for troops was " not as big as it was two weeks ago because more than a half million people quit the camp to go back home. But arriving home, it's still a big problem because they will still need humanitarian aid."

According to diplomats at the New York meeting, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State George Moose said it was important to identify where the refugees were and at the same time continue planning for a multinational force.

Decisions on military planning, however, will not come before a meeting in Stuttgart, Germany, on Friday when the makeup of a possible force will be discussed and more intelligence is gathered on the refugees.
Since last Friday Hutu refugees have begun streaming into Rwanda, causing some nations, especially the United States, to question the need to put ground troops in eastern Zaire.

Hundreds of thousands of Hutus fled back into Rwanda to escape fighting between Zairian rebels, supported by Rwanda, and soldiers from Rwanda's Hutu-dominated former army, who organized the 1994 Rwandan genocide of minority Tutsis.

Smith also said the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and other aid agencies believed troops were still needed because a majority of the refugees were still in Zaire and aid agencies could be caught in clashes.

But he said the Rwanda government remained convinced that a multinational force was not required. "It is clear that the Rwanda government has to provide cooperation (and) their position is obviously important."
He said the sovereignty of Zaire had to be respected but that foreign officials also had to deal with the rebels.

"There is the need to respect the sovereignty of Zaire and a recognition that one has to deal with those that are in fact in control in the parts of Zaire in which a force, if there was one found to be needed, would operate," he said.
"So the military planning goes ahead. The purpose is to avoid delays so that when the decision is taken, the military plans will be drawn up," he added.

According to participants at the meeting a dispute broke out between Rwanda's representatives and Soren Jessen-Petersen of UNHCR about how many refugees had returned, with Rwanda insisting the number was closer to a million and Jessen-Petersen saying 700,000 were still in Zaire.
